claims.text: The initial Mg-containing high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing material.
Rapid solidification or equivalent processing can produce the specified metastable initial state.
Controlled thermal exposure causes the metastable alloy to decompose by diffusion-mediated phase separation.
The decomposition produces Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Brief moderate annealing produces fine, uniformly distributed precipitates.
Fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates act as local diffusion barriers.
Fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates provide nucleation sites for protective oxide scales.
Moderate annealing promotes a more adherent and protective oxide scale than occurs in the as-cast metastable state.
The improved oxide scale and interfacial characteristics enhance high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The improved oxide scale and interfacial characteristics enhance corrosion resistance in subsequent corrosion testing.
Prolonged thermal exposure causes the Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates to coarsen.
Coarsened intermetallics introduce microstructural heterogeneities that act as localized corrosion sites.
Intermetallic coarsening causes corrosion resistance to decline relative to the moderately annealed condition.
Intermetallic coarsening causes high-temperature oxidation resistance to decline relative to the moderately annealed condition.
A high-temperature service regime of approximately 600–750 °C is relevant to the proposed annealing comparison.
A critical annealing time-temperature threshold separates fine-precipitate formation from precipitate coarsening.
Precipitate spacing below approximately 1 µm is associated with improved corrosion and oxidation performance.
Performance degrades after precipitate spacing or coarsening passes the proposed threshold.
